title: Why I Hate Beautiful Books
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau mounts a provocative argument against the beautiful, well-organized exercise book — a fixture praised by inspectors and school leaders — contending that it is one of the most educationally misleading artifacts in schools. The article identifies the seduction of inspectability: exercise books are solid, available, full of visible markers of activity, and can be flicked through to produce the impression that learning has occurred. But Didau argues this inspectability is precisely the problem — beautiful books are optimized for appearing learning-rich rather than for generating it. Drawing on cognitive science, the piece shows that the activities producing beautiful books (neat copying, careful color-coding, elaborately presented diagrams) are often lowest-value cognitively, while the activities producing lasting learning (wrestling with difficulty, making and correcting errors, effortful retrieval) tend to make books look messier. Didau concludes that schools prioritizing beautiful books inadvertently signal to teachers and students that presentation matters more than cognition — a distortion with serious consequences for what actually happens during learning.
points: The beautiful exercise book is an inspection artifact masquerading as evidence of learning; its neatness signals effort spent on presentation rather than on the cognitive work that produces durable knowledge.

Didau applies the performance-vs-learning distinction: activities that make books look impressive correlate weakly with long-term retention, while desirable difficulties that genuinely consolidate memory tend to produce messier-looking pages.

School leaders who prize beautiful books create a perverse incentive structure that pressures teachers to optimize for visual appeal over instructional quality — distorting both teacher behavior and student effort.

The inspectable artifact problem is general: any evidence format that can be produced cheaply and presented convincingly will be gamed, systematically undermining its diagnostic value as a proxy for actual learning.

The corrective is evaluative rather than structural — not abolishing books but asking the right questions: 'Is there evidence of hard thinking here?' rather than 'Does this look like learning happened?'
quotes: An exercise book is so temptingly inspectable. It sits there, solid and available, full of dates, titles, diagrams, worksheets, corrections, and comments in variously coloured pens. You can pick it up, flick through it and feel you’ve seen something.

They tell us what to notice before we’ve had a chance to think. If there’s a box to tick about marking frequency, coloured pens, written responses, presentation or evidence of progress, what matters has been pre-determined. The best we can hope to find is what we were looking for in the first place.

Pride” isn’t equally easy for every student to display in the approved form. For some, neatness is cheap: they can write quickly, organise space, copy accurately and still attend to the explanation. For others, the same requirements consume the working memory we’d rather they spent on the subject.

If the lesson ends with everyone having copied the teacher’s answer, the most important part of the sequence has probably been skipped. The “we do” phase should involve students making decisions with support, and the “you do” phase should require them to attempt something independently. Copying a sentence prompt, or a paragraph plan can help prepare students for independent work, but it can’t replace it.

This is especially damaging when students are asked to write at length before they know enough to write well. They fill pages with clumsy sentences, vague claims, weak evidence, bolted-on quotations and half-formed explanations. The result may look like effort, but it can easily become rehearsal in doing the wrong thing.

Before we argue about whether exercise books should be beautiful, we need to ask a simpler question: what are they for? The answer’s less obvious than it seems because schools often expect books to do several incompatible jobs. In a single subject they may be a place to think, a record of practice, a revision resource and evidence for accountability purposes.
